A tape unwinds with speed v from a roll rotating about a fixed axis with constant angular velocity. The radius of the roll r is decreasing at a steady rate.

questions.stemText: A tape unwinds with speed v from a roll rotating about a fixed axis with constant angular velocity. The radius of the roll r is decreasing at a steady rate. v r Which of the following graphs best represents the variation with time t of the speed v of the tape? A v 0 t B v 0 t C v t 0 D v 0 t
questions.difficultyReason: Students must translate the steady decrease in radius into the shape of a speed–time graph.
questions.misconception: Equating constant angular velocity with constant linear speed

explanation.body: The tape speed is $v=r\omega$. With constant $\omega$ and a radius that decreases at a steady rate, the graph is a straight line with a negative gradient. The speed stays above zero while the radius is positive.

perOption.A: Confuses constant angular velocity with constant tape speed.
perOption.B: Shows the speed dropping more slowly over time, which would require the radius to shrink more slowly.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Shows the speed dropping faster over time, which would require the radius to shrink faster.

questions.stem:
Three identical slotted masses are placed at 2R, 4R and 6R respectively from the centre of a horizontal rough disc of radius 10R.

The disc rotates about its centre O.

Which statement is correct?
questions.stemText: Three identical slotted masses are placed at 2R, 4R and 6R respectively from the centre of a horizontal rough disc of radius 10R. The disc rotates about its centre O. Which statement is correct? A All three slotted masses experience the same centripetal force. B The slotted mass at 6R is most likely to move out of its circular path. C The slotted mass at 2R completes the least number of revolutions per unit time. D The slotted mass at 6R has three times the amount of kinetic energy as the slotted mass at 2R.

options.label: A
options.text: All three slotted masses experience the same centripetal force.

options.label: B
options.text: The slotted mass at 6R is most likely to move out of its circular path.

options.label: C
options.text: The slotted mass at 2R completes the least number of revolutions per unit time.

options.label: D
options.text: The slotted mass at 6R has three times the amount of kinetic energy as the slotted mass at 2R.

appearances.originalFile: grail:10416 ACJC 2023 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Students must distinguish shared angular speed from radius-dependent speed and centripetal force.
questions.misconception: Confusing linear speed and angular speed.

explanation.body: The masses share the disc’s angular speed $\omega$ while they rotate with it. Static friction supplies the required centripetal force $mr\omega^2$, which is greatest at $6R$. For identical masses on the same surface, the maximum static friction is the same, so the outermost mass reaches that limit first.

perOption.A: At fixed angular speed, the required centripetal force increases with radius.
perOption.B: Correct. The mass at $6R$ requires the greatest static friction.
perOption.C: All three masses complete the same number of revolutions per unit time while co-rotating.
perOption.D: Kinetic energy scales with the square of linear speed, giving a factor of nine.

questions.difficultyReason: The only calculation is dividing one revolution in radians by the 12-hour period in seconds.
questions.misconception: Using the minute hand's period.

explanation.body: The hour hand takes $T=12\times60\times60\ \mathrm{s}$ to complete one revolution. Its angular speed is $\omega=2\pi/T\approx1.5\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses a six-hour period, doubling the angular speed.
perOption.C: Uses the one-hour period of the minute hand.

linear speed | centripetal acceleration

B halved | doubled
C constant | constant
D constant | doubled

appearances.originalFile: grail:14529 (ACJC) 2024 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must apply both changes and account for the square of angular speed in the acceleration.
questions.misconception: Assuming unchanged linear speed means unchanged centripetal acceleration.

explanation.body: The linear speed is $v=r\omega$ and the centripetal acceleration is $a=\omega^2r$. With radius $r/2$ and angular speed $2\omega$, the new linear speed is $(r/2)(2\omega)=v$. The new centripetal acceleration is $(r/2)(2\omega)^2=2a$.

perOption.A: Ignores the doubled angular speed in the speed calculation and misses the doubling of acceleration.
perOption.B: Accounts for the smaller radius alone when calculating the linear speed.
perOption.C: Treats the acceleration as constant because the linear speed stays constant, overlooking the halved radius.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A particle moves at a constant speed in a circular path.

If the radius of the path is doubled while the period of rotation remains the same, what happens to the centripetal acceleration?
questions.stemText: A particle moves at a constant speed in a circular path. If the radius of the path is doubled while the period of rotation remains the same, what happens to the centripetal acceleration? A It increases by a factor of 4. B It is doubled. C It is halved. D It remains the same.

options.label: A
options.text: It increases by a factor of 4.

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Choose the right form of the acceleration formula when the period is fixed.
questions.misconception: Using $a = v^2/r$ while treating $v$ as constant

explanation.body:
$a_c = r\omega^2 = r\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{T}\right)^2$.

With $T$ unchanged, $a_c \propto r$, so doubling $r$ gives $a_{\text{new}} = 2a_c$.

perOption.A: Treats $a = v^2/r$ as $\propto v^2$ only, forgetting that $r$ also doubles in the denominator.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses $a = v^2/r$ with $v$ held constant, but $v = 2\pi r/T$ doubles.
perOption.D: Ignores the dependence on $r$ at fixed period.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Titan, the largest moon of Saturn, orbits in a circle around Saturn with a radius of 1.22 × $10^{6}$ km. It has an orbital period of 15.9 days.

What is the centripetal acceleration of Titan?
questions.stemText: Titan, the largest moon of Saturn, orbits in a circle around Saturn with a radius of 1.22 × 106 km. It has an orbital period of 15.9 days. What is the centripetal acceleration of Titan? A 4.06 × $10^{-3}$ m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ B 2.55 × $10^{-2}$ m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ C 9.19 × $10^{-2}$ m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ D 1.55 × $10^{3}$ m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$
questions.difficultyReason: The student must convert the orbital data to SI units and use angular speed in the acceleration formula.
questions.misconception: Omitting a factor of $2\pi$ when converting period to angular speed.

explanation.body: Convert the radius to $1.22\times10^9\ \mathrm{m}$ and the period to $(15.9)(24)(3600)\ \mathrm{s}$. Using $a=r\omega^2$ gives $a=(1.22\times10^9)\left[\frac{2\pi}{(15.9)(24)(3600)}\right]^2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\approx2.55\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

perOption.A: Omits one factor of $2\pi$ in the squared angular-speed term.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Arises from leaving the radius in kilometres and converting the period to minutes.
perOption.D: Would require an angular speed much greater than the given orbital period implies.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A record on a turntable rotates at a constant number of revolutions per second.

Which graph best represents the relationship between the linear speed v of a point on the record and its distance r from the centre of the rotation?

questions.difficultyReason: One direct proportionality determines the shape and intercept of the graph.
questions.misconception: Confusing a common angular speed with a common linear speed.

explanation.body: All points on the record have the same constant angular speed $\omega$. Since $v=r\omega$, linear speed is directly proportional to radius and the graph is a straight line through the origin.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Treats the common angular speed as a common linear speed.
perOption.C: Shows speed decreasing as the radius increases.
perOption.D: Shows the slope decreasing even though it equals the constant angular speed.

perOption.A: Uses one revolution as one radian, omitting the factor of 2π.
perOption.B: Uses a 24-hour period for the hour hand.
perOption.C: Correct. It uses one full turn in 12 hours.
perOption.D: Uses the minute hand’s one-hour period.

questions.difficultyReason: Students must convert angular speed to a period and identify the separation after one and a half turns.
questions.misconception: Confusing displacement with distance along a circular path.

explanation.body: The period is $T=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/2}=4\ \mathrm{s}$. After $6.0\ \mathrm{s}$ the marble has made 1.5 revolutions, so it is directly opposite P and its displacement has magnitude $2r=2(0.80)=1.6\ \mathrm{m}$.

questions.stem:

questions.stemText: A drone is performing a vertical circular path stunt for its audience on the ground. Which diagram shows the resultant acceleration a acting on the drone at the instant where its velocity is V and speeding up? A V a B V a C V a D V a

appearances.originalFile: grail:18733 ASRJC 2025 Prelim P1 H2 Physics QN paper

questions.difficultyReason: The student must combine inward acceleration with acceleration along the direction of motion.
questions.misconception: Assuming acceleration in circular motion is always entirely centripetal

explanation.body: At the top of the path, the vertical component is the centripetal acceleration and points down toward the centre. The horizontal component points to the right, along the velocity, because the drone is speeding up. The resultant therefore points down and to the right.

perOption.A: Shows only the centripetal component, so the speed is instantaneously constant.
perOption.B: The leftward component is opposite the velocity and would slow the drone down.
perOption.C: Shows only tangential acceleration and omits the inward component needed to turn.

questions.stem:
A small object of mass m is suspended from a fixed point O by a light, inextensible cord. The object is raised until the cord is horizontal and then released. It moves in an arc of a circle as shown in the figure.

What is the tension in the cord when it passes through its lowest position at point P?
questions.stemText: A small object of mass m is suspended from a fixed point O by a light, inextensible cord. The object is raised until the cord is horizontal and then released. It moves in an arc of a circle as shown in the figure. m O P What is the tension in the cord when it passes through its lowest position at point P? A zero B mg C 2mg D 3mg

appearances.originalFile: ASRJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1 for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Combine energy conservation for speed with Newton's second law for circular motion.
questions.misconception: Taking tension at the lowest point to equal the weight

explanation.body: Let $r$ be the cord length. The drop to P converts gravitational potential energy into kinetic energy, so $mgr=\tfrac12 mv^2$ and $v=\sqrt{2gr}$. At P, $T-mg=mv^2/r=2mg$. Hence $T=3mg$.

perOption.A: Assumes the cord has no tension at the bottom of the swing.
perOption.B: Balances the weight and leaves no inward resultant.
perOption.C: Uses the inward resultant force as the tension.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.stem:
An object of mass m is attached to a rigid rod and spun in a uniform vertical circular motion with radius r and a linear velocity of v.

What is the variation of the magnitude of the centripetal acceleration of the object over one revolution?
questions.stemText: An object of mass m is attached to a rigid rod and spun in a uniform vertical circular motion with radius r and a linear velocity of v. What is the variation of the magnitude of the centripetal acceleration of the object over one revolution? A zero B 2g C v 2 r D v 2 2 r

appearances.originalFile: grail:16130 2022 H2 CJC Physics Promo Paper 1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: Distinguishes a vector's constant magnitude from its changing direction.
questions.misconception: Confusing acceleration magnitude with its change

explanation.body: The speed $v$ remains constant in uniform circular motion. With fixed radius $r$, the magnitude $a_{\mathrm{c}}=v^2/r$ stays constant, so its variation over a revolution is zero.

perOption.A: Correct. The magnitude stays constant throughout the revolution.
perOption.B: Confuses gravity's effect on the rod force with a change in centripetal acceleration magnitude.
perOption.C: Gives the constant magnitude itself.
perOption.D: Uses the difference between opposite acceleration vectors when the question asks about changes in magnitude.

questions.stemText:
A ribbon, wound around a reel, is pulled and rotates about its centre. The ribbon leaves the reel at a constant $v$ and at a variable distance $r$ from the centre of the reel as shown.

[Diagram: Two views show the ribbon unwinding tangentially to the right with speed $v$. The lower view labels the radius $r$ from the reel centre to the wound ribbon.]

What is the relationship between the angular velocity of the reel and the variable distance $r$ from the centre of the reel?

B  Angular velocity is proportional to $\frac{1}{r}$.

explanation.body: At the point where the ribbon leaves the reel, $v=r\omega$, so $\omega=v/r$. Since $v$ is constant, $\omega$ is proportional to $1/r$.

perOption.A: The speed relation contains one power of the radius.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: This reverses the dependence obtained by solving for angular velocity.

An object of mass $m$ and weight $W$ is fixed to one end of a light rod which rotates in a vertical circle of radius $r$. The object has an angular velocity $\omega$ when it is vertically below the centre of the circle.

[Diagram: A vertical rod joins the centre of a dashed circle to the object at the bottom. The circle is labelled with radius $r$, the object with mass $m$ and weight $W$, and a clockwise arrow with $\omega$.]

What is the tension in the rod acting upwards on the object when the object is vertically below the centre of the circle?

A  $W+mr\omega^2$
B  $W-mr\omega^2$
C  $mr\omega^2-W$
D  $mr\omega^2$

questions.difficultyReason: Students identify the inward direction and include both vertical forces.
questions.misconception: Treating tension alone as the centripetal force

explanation.body: At the bottom of the circle, the upward tension $T$ minus the downward weight $W$ provides the centripetal force. Thus $T-W=mr\omega^2$, giving $T=W+mr\omega^2$.

questions.stem:
An object of mass m moves in a circular path of radius r at a constant angular speed ω.

What is the work done by the centripetal force on the object?
questions.stemText: An object of mass m moves in a circular path of radius r at a constant angular speed ω. What is the work done by the centripetal force on the object? A zero B $r^{2}$$\omega ^{2}$ C $mr\omega ^{2}$ D $mr^{2}$$\omega ^{2}$
questions.difficultyReason: The student only needs to recognize that the centripetal force and instantaneous displacement are perpendicular.
questions.misconception: Treating radius as displacement along the force

explanation.body: The centripetal force is always perpendicular to the instantaneous velocity. It has no component along the instantaneous displacement, so it does zero work.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Gives the square of the tangential speed, which has units of energy per mass.
perOption.C: Gives the magnitude of the centripetal force in newtons.

questions.stem:
The Earth takes 24 hours to complete one rotation on its axis.

What is the angular velocity of the Earth as it rotates on its axis?
questions.stemText: The Earth takes 24 hours to complete one rotation on its axis. What is the angular velocity of the Earth as it rotates on its axis? A 1.75 x $10^{-3}$ rad $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ B 1.99 x $10^{-7}$ rad $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ C 4.36 x $10^{-3}$ rad $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ D 7.27 x $10^{-5}$ rad $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$
questions.difficultyReason: Convert one rotation to radians and the period to seconds.
questions.misconception: Using minutes in a rate expressed per second

explanation.body: One rotation is $2\pi$ radians. The angular velocity is $\omega=2\pi/T=2\pi/(24\times60\times60)=7.27\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Uses 3600 seconds as the period, omitting the factor of 24.
perOption.B: Uses approximately the period of Earth’s orbit around the Sun.
perOption.C: Divides by the period in minutes and reports the result in $\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A stone is attached to a string. The stone is then caused to swing in a vertical circular motion at a constant speed.

Which of the following statements is incorrect?
questions.stemText: A stone is attached to a string. The stone is then caused to swing in a vertical circular motion at a constant speed. Which of the following statements is incorrect? A The magnitude of resultant force acting on the stone is constant throughout the circular motion. B The acceleration is always directed towards the centre of the circle throughout the circular motion. C The kinetic energy of the stone is constant throughout the circular motion. D The tension in the string when the stone is at the highest point of the circular motion is higher than that when the stone is at the lowest point.

options.label: A
options.text: The magnitude of resultant force acting on the stone is constant throughout the circular motion.

options.label: B
options.text: The acceleration is always directed towards the centre of the circle throughout the circular motion.

options.label: C
options.text: The kinetic energy of the stone is constant throughout the circular motion.

options.label: D
options.text: The tension in the string when the stone is at the highest point of the circular motion is higher than that when the stone is at the lowest point.

questions.difficultyReason: Compare the radial force balances at the top and bottom and check the other consequences of constant speed.
questions.misconception: Treating tension as the whole centripetal force

explanation.body:
The centripetal force has constant magnitude, and the acceleration always points towards the centre. The kinetic energy $\tfrac12 mv^2$ is constant because the speed is constant.

At the lowest point, $T-mg=F_{\mathrm c}$, so $T=F_{\mathrm c}+mg$. At the highest point, $T+mg=F_{\mathrm c}$, so $T=F_{\mathrm c}-mg$. The tension is therefore lower at the highest point.

perOption.A: This statement is true because $mv^2/r$ has constant magnitude.
perOption.B: This statement is true because the acceleration is centripetal.
perOption.C: This statement is true because $\tfrac12 mv^2$ is constant.
perOption.D: Correct. The stated tension comparison is reversed.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A body is moving in a circular path with a radius of 7.70 cm. The time for one orbit is 2.36 s.

What is the centripetal acceleration of the body?
questions.stemText: A body is moving in a circular path with a radius of 7.70 cm. The time for one orbit is 2.36 s. What is the centripetal acceleration of the body? A 0.109 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ B 0.206 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ C 0.368 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ D 0.546 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$
questions.difficultyReason: Straight substitution into a = rω² with ω = 2π/T and a unit conversion.
questions.misconception: Forgetting the cm to m conversion or omitting 2π

explanation.body: The centripetal acceleration is $a=r\omega^2=r(2\pi/T)^2$. With $r=7.70\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm m$ and $T=2.36\ \mathrm s$, this gives $a=0.546\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

perOption.A: Underestimates the acceleration by using too small a value for the squared angular speed.
perOption.B: The value is $r\omega$, which is the tangential speed in metres per second.
perOption.C: Underestimates the acceleration given by multiplying the radius by the squared angular speed.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.stemText:
An object tied to the end of a light inextensible string of length $25\ \mathrm{cm}$ is swung in a vertical circle as shown.

[A dashed vertical circle shows the object at the top, right, bottom and left, with clockwise arrows and a radius labelled $25\ \mathrm{cm}$.]

questions.difficultyReason: Students must relate the tension differences in three rod segments to the individual centripetal forces.
questions.misconception: Using the same orbital radius for all three masses

explanation.body: Let $T_1$, $T_2$ and $T_3$ be the tensions in the rightmost, middle and leftmost segments. For the rightmost mass, $T_1=4.0\omega^2$, and the middle and leftmost masses give $T_2-T_1=3.0\omega^2$ and $T_3-T_2=2.0\omega^2$. Thus $T_3=9.0\omega^2=9.0(2.0)^2=36\ \mathrm{N}$, the magnitude of the force the rod exerts on the pivot.

perOption.A: Falls below even the $8\ \mathrm{N}$ centripetal force needed for the innermost mass.

questions.stemText: Two stars of masses M and 2M move in circular motion about their common centre of mass. Which of the following statements is true? A Such a motion is not possible. options.label: A

A car of mass $1000\ \mathrm{kg}$ turns with a circular radius of $100\ \mathrm{m}$ on a slope banked at $30^\circ$. The car has a constant speed of $90\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}$. What is the sidewards frictional force acting on the tyres?

A 508 N, downwards along the slope
B 508 N, upwards along the slope
C 6250 N, downwards along the slope
D 6250 N, upwards along the slope

stemImage.alt: Question 17: A car of mass 1000 kg turns with a circular radius of 100 m on a slope banked at 30. The car has a constant speed of 90 km h1. What is the sidewards frictiona

appearances.originalFile: grail:12812 EJC 2021 J1 H2 Promo P1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: The student must resolve two contact forces and solve simultaneous component equations.
questions.misconception: Equating friction with the net centripetal force

explanation.body: With friction $f$ acting down the slope, the horizontal force equation is $f\cos\theta+N\sin\theta=mv^2/r$. Vertically, $N\cos\theta=mg+f\sin\theta$. Dividing the rearranged horizontal equation by the vertical equation gives $\tan\theta=(mv^2/r-f\cos\theta)/(mg+f\sin\theta)$. Using $v=90000/3600=25\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and $\theta=30^\circ$ gives $f=508\ \mathrm{N}$ down the slope.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Upslope friction would reduce the available inward force at this speed.
perOption.C: Uses the entire centripetal force as friction along the slope.
perOption.D: Uses the entire centripetal force as friction and reverses its direction.

questions.stem:
Three identical masses are tied using light, inextensible strings of equal lengths r to a pin and made to rotate around the pin by sliding over a smooth horizontal table as shown in the diagram. The strings remain along a straight line as the masses rotate.

What is the ratio of tensions in string 1 : string 2 : string 3?
questions.stemText: Three identical masses are tied using light, inextensible strings of equal lengths r to a pin and made to rotate around the pin by sliding over a smooth horizontal table as shown in the diagram. The strings remain along a straight line as the masses rotate. r r r pin mass mass What is the ratio of tensions in string 1 : string 2 : string 3? A 1 : 2 : 3 B 3 : 2 : 1 C 3 : 5 : 6 D 6 : 5 : 3
questions.difficultyReason: Requires using the net inward force on each mass to build up the three tensions.
questions.misconception: Equating each tension to the centripetal force of only one mass

explanation.body: The outer mass has $T_3=m(3r)\omega^2$. For the middle mass, $T_2-T_3=m(2r)\omega^2$, so $T_2=5mr\omega^2$. For the inner mass, $T_1-T_2=mr\omega^2$, so $T_1=6mr\omega^2$ and the ratio is $6:5:3$.

perOption.A: Treats each string’s tension as the centripetal force on just one mass, making string 1 the weakest.
perOption.B: Makes string 1 the largest but gives a ratio of 3 to 1 for the inner and outer tensions instead of 2 to 1.
perOption.C: Reverses the ratio even though string 1 provides the centripetal force for all three masses.
perOption.D: Correct.

$N$ is the normal reaction and $f$ is the frictional force.

A. $f$ points down-left and $mv^2/r$ points horizontally left.
B. $f$ points down-left and $mv^2/r$ points horizontally right.
C. $f$ points up-right and $mv^2/r$ points down-left.
D. $f$ points down-left. There is no $mv^2/r$ arrow.]

questions.difficultyReason: Identify the individual forces and recognize their centripetal resultant.
questions.misconception: Drawing the centripetal resultant as an extra force.

explanation.body: The free-body diagram shows the weight, normal reaction and any friction along the road. The centripetal force is their inward resultant, so it is omitted as a separate arrow. Friction’s direction along the bank depends on the car’s speed.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A turntable rotates about a fixed axis starting with angular velocity that is increasing steadily over time. P and Q are fixed points on the turntable.

[Top view of a circular turntable. P is nearer the centre and Q is near the upper-right edge.]

Which one of the graphs below correctly shows how the centripetal acceleration $a$ for P and Q vary with time $t$?

[Each graph plots $a$ vertically against $t$ horizontally, with Q above P and both starting at positive $a$.
A. Two rising concave-up curves with approximately constant vertical separation.
B. Two rising straight lines, with Q steeper than P.
C. Two rising concave-up curves, with Q steepening more and pulling farther above P.
D. Two parallel rising straight lines.]

stemImage.alt: Question 16: A turntable rotates about a fixed axis starting with angular velocity that is increasing steadily over time. P and Q are fixed points on the turntable. Q P Whic

appearances.originalFile: grail:12817 EJC 2022 J1 H2 PROMO QP PAPER 1

questions.difficultyReason: Use the squared angular speed to infer curvature and compare accelerations at two radii.
questions.misconception: Assuming centripetal acceleration increases linearly with angular speed.

explanation.body: The centripetal acceleration is $a=r\omega^2$, so a steadily increasing $\omega$ gives an upward-curving quadratic in time. Both points have the same $\omega$ at each instant, so $a_P/a_Q=r_P/r_Q$ is constant. Since $r_Q>r_P$, Q has the greater acceleration and the steeper curve.

perOption.A: Shows approximately equal slopes, whereas the larger radius gives Q a greater rate of increase.
perOption.B: Shows linear growth in time, which misses the square of the angular velocity.
perOption.C: Correct. Q’s curve rises faster while both curves grow quadratically.
perOption.D: Shows linear growth and equal slopes, missing both the squared dependence and the radius dependence.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Two identical masses P and Q are attached to two strings of length $r$ each as shown in the figure below. P, Q and X remain collinear as the masses execute a uniform circular motion.

[From left to right, the diagram shows X, P and Q on a straight line. XP and PQ are each labelled $r$. A dashed orbit passes through Q and is centred on X.]

Which of the following statements is true?
A. The tension in the string along XP is larger than that along PQ.
B. The angular velocity experienced by mass Q is larger than that experienced by mass P.
C. The linear velocity experienced by mass P is larger than that experienced by mass Q.
D. The centripetal acceleration experienced by mass P is larger than that experienced by mass Q.

appearances.originalFile: grail:12817 EJC 2022 J1 H2 PROMO QP PAPER 1

questions.difficultyReason: It requires separate radial force balances for the two masses.
questions.misconception: Treating each string tension as the net force

explanation.body: For Q, the only radial force is $T_{PQ}=m\omega^2(2r)$. For P, the inward tension must overcome the outward pull of PQ and provide the centripetal force, so $T_{XP}-T_{PQ}=m\omega^2r$. Hence $T_{XP}=3m\omega^2r>T_{PQ}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: P and Q share the same angular velocity because they remain collinear with X.
perOption.C: Q has the larger speed because $v=\omega r$ at the same angular velocity.
perOption.D: Q has the larger centripetal acceleration because $a=\omega^2r$ at the same angular velocity.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A car is driven round an icy road banked at an angle $\theta$ of $25^\circ$ and a radius $r$ of $50\ \mathrm{m}$ as shown.

[A car is on a banked circular bend. The bank angle $\theta$ is marked against a horizontal reference line and the horizontal radius $r$ extends from the car to the marked centre.]

The frictional force between the tyres and the road is negligible.

What is the speed that the car can travel at while maintaining the circular radius?

A $2.6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
B $7.3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
C $15.1\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
D $21.9\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$

stemImage.alt: Question 8: A car is driven round an icy road banked at an angle θ of 25o and a radius r of 50 m as shown. The frictional force between the tyres and the road is negligible

appearances.originalFile: grail:10429 EJC 2023 J2 H2 PRELIM P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must resolve the normal force along two axes to eliminate it.
questions.misconception: Using the whole normal force as the centripetal force

explanation.body:
The horizontal component of the normal force supplies the centripetal force, so $N\sin\theta=mv^2/r$. Vertical equilibrium gives $N\cos\theta=mg$.

Dividing gives $\tan\theta=v^2/(rg)$, hence $v=\sqrt{50(9.81)\tan25^\circ}=15.1\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: This would require a much smaller inward force than the bank provides.
perOption.B: Using this speed confuses the tangent factor in $v^2$ with a factor applied directly to $v$.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: This is close to treating the full weight as the inward force and misses the factor $\tan25^\circ$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
An object of $3.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ is fixed to one end of a light rod which rotates freely in a vertical circle. The length of the rod is $7.7\ \mathrm{m}$.

[A dashed vertical circle surrounds the pivot. The rod extends down and right from the pivot to the object and makes angle $\theta$ with the downward vertical. A curved arrow near the object indicates anticlockwise rotation.]

When $\theta$ is $30^\circ$, the speed of the object is $25.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Assume that there is no energy loss to the surrounding.

Which of the following describes the force in the rod when the object is at the top of the circular motion?

A $94\ \mathrm{N}$ in compression
B $94\ \mathrm{N}$ in tension
C $121\ \mathrm{N}$ in compression
D $121\ \mathrm{N}$ in tension

stemImage.alt: Question 9: An object of 3.5 kg is fixed to one end of a light rod which rotates freely in a vertical circle. The length of the rod is 7.7 m. When θ is 30o, the speed of th

appearances.originalFile: grail:10429 EJC 2023 J2 H2 PRELIM P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must use the diagram to find the height gain, then combine energy conservation and radial dynamics.
questions.misconception: Equating the rod force to the net centripetal force

explanation.body:
The gain in gravitational potential energy equals the loss of kinetic energy, so $mgr(1+\cos\theta)=\frac12m(v_i^2-v_f^2)$. Substituting gives $(9.81)(7.7)(1+\cos30^\circ)=\frac12(25^2-v_f^2)$, hence $v_f=18.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

Assume the rod is in tension, so both weight and the rod force point towards the centre at the top. Then $(3.5)(9.81)+F=3.5(18.5)^2/7.7$, giving $F=121\ \mathrm{N}$ in tension.

perOption.A: Using $94\,\mathrm{N}$ underestimates the required rod force, and compression would push the object away from the centre.
perOption.B: The direction is right, but this force plus the weight falls short of the required centripetal force.
perOption.C: The magnitude is right, but the rod must pull towards the centre at the top.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A mass $m_1$ is attached to one end of an elastic string of an unstretched length $L$. When the mass is rotating with a linear speed $v$ on a smooth table in a horizontal circle, an extension $e$ is obtained.

Which of the following shows the correct expression for mass $m_2$, attached to the end of the same string, if it is rotated with the same linear speed $v$ but twice the radius as that produced by $m_1$?

A $m_2=\frac{2m_1(L+2e)}{e}$
B $m_2=\frac{2m_1(L+e)}{e}$
C $m_2=\frac{2m_1(2L+e)}{e}$
D $m_2=\frac{2m_1(2L+2e)}{e}$

stemImage.alt: Question 13: A mass m1 is attached to one end of an elastic string of an unstretched length L. When the mass is rotating with a linear speed v on a smooth table in a horizon

appearances.originalFile: grail:12822 EJC 2023 J1 H2 Promo P1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: Students must relate mass to both orbital radius and string extension at fixed speed.
questions.misconception: Treating the stretched length as the extension.

explanation.body: The elastic tension provides the centripetal force, so for extension $\Delta L$, $k\Delta L=mv^2/r$. With $k$ and $v$ fixed, $m\propto r\Delta L$. The radius doubles from $L+e$ to $2(L+e)$, so the new extension is $2(L+e)-L=L+2e$. Hence $\frac{m_2}{m_1}=2\frac{L+2e}{e}$ and $m_2=\frac{2m_1(L+2e)}{e}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses the original radius $L+e$ as the new extension.
perOption.C: Doubles the natural-length term in the new extension instead of doubling the original extension term.
perOption.D: Uses the new stretched length as the new extension.

questions.stemText:
A ball of mass $m$ is attached to a rope. The ball is rotating in a vertical circle of radius $L$ with a constant frequency $f$ as shown. The acceleration of free fall is $g$.

[The ball is shown at the upper right of a dashed vertical circle, joined to its centre by the rope. A curved arrow labelled $f$ indicates anticlockwise rotation, and a radius is labelled $L$.]

What is the maximum variation in the magnitude of the tension in the string during one revolution of the stone?

A $0$
B $2mg$
C $2\pi^2 f^2mL$
D $4\pi^2 f^2mL$

appearances.originalFile: grail:12822 EJC 2023 J1 H2 Promo P1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: Students must resolve weight in opposite radial directions and compare two tension equations.
questions.misconception: Equating the rope tension with the centripetal force.

explanation.body: The resultant of tension and weight provides the centripetal force. At the top, $mL(2\pi f)^2=T_{\mathrm{top}}+mg$. At the bottom, $mL(2\pi f)^2=T_{\mathrm{bottom}}-mg$. Subtracting the two equations gives $T_{\mathrm{bottom}}-T_{\mathrm{top}}=2mg$.

perOption.A: Assumes that a constant centripetal force means a constant tension.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Takes half the centripetal force as the change in tension, overlooking the opposite radial contributions of weight.
perOption.D: Uses the whole centripetal force as the change in tension.

A small ring, of mass $m$, moves along a smooth circular track in the vertical plane, as shown in the figure below. P is the centre of the circular track.

[The ring is shown at the top and bottom of a vertical circular track. A radius from P is labelled $1.0\ \mathrm{m}$. An arrow on the right shows anticlockwise motion.]

The radius of the track is $1.0\ \mathrm{m}$.
At the bottom of the track, an upward normal force of magnitude $5.5mg$ acts on the small ring.
Which row correctly describes the magnitude and direction of the normal force acting on the small ring when it is at the top of the track?

A $0.5mg$, upwards
B $0.5mg$, downwards
C $1.5mg$, upwards
D $1.5mg$, downwards

appearances.originalFile: grail:14539 (EJC) 2024 J2 H2 PRELIM QP P1

questions.difficultyReason: You must combine two radial force equations with conservation of energy and interpret the sign of the normal force.
questions.misconception: Assuming that the normal force must point inward.

explanation.body: At the bottom, $N_B-mg=mv_B^2/r$. At the top, assume $N_T$ points downwards, so $N_T+mg=mv_T^2/r$. Conservation of energy gives $mg(2r)=\tfrac12m(v_B^2-v_T^2)$. Subtracting the top force equation from the bottom one and substituting the energy relation gives $N_B-N_T=6mg$. Since $N_B=5.5mg$, $N_T=-0.5mg$ under the downward convention, so the normal force is $0.5mg$ upwards.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Treats the negative result in the downward convention as a downward force.
perOption.C: Adds the required inward resultant to the weight when calculating the upward force.
perOption.D: Adds the weight to the required inward resultant and assigns the sum to a downward normal force.

questions.stem:
A steel sphere is set in motion so that it is moving in a horizontal circle at constant speed with a radius r, as shown below.

The distance from the centre of the sphere to the top of the spring is 10.8 cm and the spring is tilted at 27° from the vertical.

What is the period of the circular motion of the sphere?
questions.stemText: A steel sphere is set in motion so that it is moving in a horizontal circle at constant speed with a radius r, as shown below. The distance from the centre of the sphere to the top of the spring is 10.8 cm and the spring is tilted at 27° from the vertical. What is the period of the circular motion of the sphere? A 0.62 s B 7.9 s C 6.2 s D 79 s

appearances.originalFile: grail:19933 EJC 2025 J2 H2 PRELIM P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must resolve the spring force, obtain the orbit radius and combine the equations to find the period.
questions.misconception: Using the spring-to-sphere distance as the orbital radius

explanation.body:
The vertical component of the spring tension balances the weight, so $kx\cos\theta=mg$. Its horizontal component provides the centripetal force, so $kx\sin\theta=mr(2\pi/T)^2$.

Dividing the equations and using $r=0.108\sin27^\circ$ gives $\tan27^\circ=\frac{4\pi^2(0.108\sin27^\circ)}{T^2(9.81)}$, so $T=0.62\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The two components of spring tension determine the period.
perOption.B: This period gives a centripetal force too small for the horizontal component of tension.
perOption.C: Treats $10.8\ \mathrm{cm}$ as $10.8\ \mathrm{m}$, making the period ten times too large.
perOption.D: This period would require a much larger orbital radius at the stated angle.

A. zero

questions.difficultyReason: This requires subtracting two equal tangential velocities inclined at 60°.
questions.misconception: Confusing constant speed with constant velocity

explanation.body: The fixed radius and constant angular velocity give the same speed $v=r\omega$ at A and B. The velocity vectors are $60^\circ$ apart, so the triangle formed by the vectors and their difference is equilateral. Thus $|\Delta\mathbf v|=v=r\omega$.

perOption.A: This treats constant speed as constant velocity.
perOption.B: This gives half the side representing the velocity change.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: This adds the speeds as if the velocity vectors were opposite.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: A part in an engine is rotating in a circle of radius 8.0 cm at 3000 revolutions per minute. What is its centripetal acceleration?
questions.stemText: A part in an engine is rotating in a circle of radius 8.0 cm at 3000 revolutions per minute. What is its centripetal acceleration? A 25 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ B 7900 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ C 3.1 x $10^{4}$ m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ D 7.2 x $10^{7}$ m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$
questions.difficultyReason: Requires two unit conversions and one substitution.
questions.misconception: Using rpm directly as angular speed.

explanation.body: Use $a=\omega^2r$, with $\omega=2\pi(3000/60)$ and $r=8.0/100\ \mathrm{m}$. This gives $a=[2\pi(3000/60)]^2(8.0/100)\approx7900\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

perOption.A: Calculates the tangential speed $\omega r$ instead.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Doubling the angular speed would quadruple the acceleration to about $3.1\times10^4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.
perOption.D: Treats rpm as radians per second and leaves the radius in centimetres.

questions.misconception: Identifying the cage force with the centripetal resultant.

explanation.body: The cage force $R$ and the person’s weight $W$ are the only forces acting. Their resultant points horizontally toward the centre of the circle, to the right. The upward component of $R$ balances the weight, and its rightward component provides the centripetal force.

perOption.A: Correct.

If the sphere is moving with a centripetal acceleration of 0.8g, what is the angle θ?
questions.stemText: A small sphere is set into circular motion in a horizontal plane within a smooth cone as shown. If the sphere is moving with a centripetal acceleration of 0.8g, what is the angle θ? A $37^{\mathrm{o}}$ B $39^{\mathrm{o}}$ C $51^{\mathrm{o}}$ D $53^{\mathrm{o}}$

appearances.originalFile: grail:20232 2025 HCI C2 Prelim H2 Physics P1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: The student must resolve the normal force using the cone’s angle to the vertical, then take a ratio.
questions.misconception: Swapping the radial and vertical components of the normal force

explanation.body: The upward component of the normal force balances the weight, so $N\sin\theta=mg$. The inward component provides the centripetal force, so $N\cos\theta=m(0.8g)$. Dividing gives $\tan\theta=1.25$, so $\theta=51.3^\circ$.

perOption.A: Uses $\cos^{-1}(0.8)$, treating $0.8$ as a component-to-normal-force ratio.
perOption.B: Swaps the sine and cosine components and obtains the complementary angle.
perOption.C: Correct. The angle is approximately $51^\circ$.
perOption.D: Uses $\sin^{-1}(0.8)$, treating $0.8$ as a component-to-normal-force ratio.

What is the net force acting on the ball when the string is horizontal?

A $2.9\ \mathrm N$

questions.difficultyReason: The student must calculate the radial force and combine it with a perpendicular tangential force.
questions.misconception: Equating the net force with the centripetal force

explanation.body: The horizontal tension supplies the centripetal force, $T=mv^2/r=(0.30)(4.0)^2/0.60=8.0\ \mathrm N$. The weight $W$ acts vertically, so the net force has magnitude $F=\sqrt{T^2+W^2}=\sqrt{8.0^2+(0.30\times9.81)^2}=8.52\ \mathrm N$.

perOption.B: Includes only the centripetal force and omits the perpendicular weight.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A mass $m_1$ is attached to one end of an elastic string of an unstretched length $L$. When the mass is rotating with a linear speed $v$ on a smooth table in a horizontal circle, an extension $e$ is obtained.

A second mass $m_2$ rotates with the same linear speed $v$. The radius is twice that produced by $m_1$.

What is the mass $m_2$?
A $\frac{2m_1(L+e)}{e}$
B $\frac{2m_1(L+2e)}{e}$
C $\frac{2m_1(2L+e)}{e}$
D $\frac{2m_1(2L+2e)}{e}$

stemImage.alt: Question 10: A mass m1 is attached to one end of an elastic string of an unstretched length L. When the mass is rotating with a linear speed v on a smooth table in a horizon

appearances.originalFile: grail:10503 2023 JPJC Prelim H2 Phy P1

questions.difficultyReason: Doubling the radius changes both its value in the centripetal force equation and the extension that sets the tension.
questions.misconception: Using the stretched length in Hooke’s law.

explanation.body: For $m_1$, $\frac{m_1v^2}{L+e}=ke$, so $v^2=\frac{ke(L+e)}{m_1}$. For $m_2$, $\frac{m_2v^2}{2(L+e)}=k[2(L+e)-L]=k(L+2e)$. Substituting for $v^2$ in $m_2=\frac{2k(L+e)(L+2e)}{v^2}$ gives $m_2=\frac{2m_1(L+2e)}{e}$.

perOption.A: Uses the first stretched length $L+e$ as the second extension.
perOption.B: Correct. The second extension is $L+2e$.
perOption.C: Doubles $L$ while leaving $e$ unchanged in the second extension.
perOption.D: Uses the entire second radius as the extension.

questions.misconception: Using the bob’s weight as the magnitude of the tension.

explanation.body: For tension $P$, the horizontal component supplies the centripetal force, $P\sin\theta=mr\omega^2$, and the vertical component balances weight, $P\cos\theta=mg$. explanation.body: The vertical component of the contact force balances weight, so $F\sin\theta=mg$. The horizontal component provides the centripetal force, so $F\cos\theta=mv^2/r$. Dividing gives $\tan\theta=gr/v^2=9.81(30)/20^2=0.73575$, hence $\theta=\tan^{-1}(0.73575)\approx36^\circ$.

questions.difficultyReason: It combines energy conservation over a two-radius rise with a radial force balance at the top.
questions.misconception: Using the bottom speed at the top

explanation.body: At the top, the kinetic energy is the initial kinetic energy minus the gain in gravitational potential energy, giving $\tfrac12(1.27)(5.75)^2-(1.27)(9.81)(1.20)=6.044\ \mathrm{J}$. From $\tfrac12 mv^2=6.044\ \mathrm{J}$, the speed there is $3.085\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. At the top, weight and tension both act towards the centre, so $T=mv^2/r-mg=(1.27)(3.085)^2/0.600-(1.27)(9.81)\approx7.69\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.B: Gives the net inward force at the top, which includes the weight.
perOption.C: Gives the net inward force computed using the bottom speed.
perOption.D: Gives the tension at the bottom, where weight acts away from the centre.

questions.stemText: A simple pendulum consists of a bob of mass m at the end of a light inextensible thread of length L. The other end of the thread is fixed at C. The bob swings through point A with velocity v and just reaches B, where the string is just taut. L C B v A What is the tension in the thread as the bob passes point A? A mg B 2mg C 3 mg D 4 mg
questions.difficultyReason: Use conservation of energy to determine the speed term, then apply the radial force equation.
questions.misconception: Equating tension to the net centripetal force

explanation.body: From A to B, the bob gains gravitational potential energy equal to its loss of kinetic energy. It rises by $L$ and comes momentarily to rest at B, so $mgL=\tfrac12mv^2$ and $mv^2=2mgL$. At A, $T-mg=mv^2/L=2mg$, giving $T=3mg$.

perOption.A: Balances tension with weight and omits the inward acceleration at A.
perOption.B: Sets the tension itself equal to $mv^2/L$, ignoring the opposing weight.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Overstates the inward resultant as $3mg$, whereas the energy calculation gives $2mg$.

If the body falls off the track as shown above, what is a possible value of v?

questions.difficultyReason: Must bound v using energy conservation: enough to rise above the centre but not enough to complete the loop.
questions.misconception: Thinking v = √(gr) at the bottom is the condition for completing the loop

explanation.body: At mid-height the limiting speed is zero, so energy conservation gives $\tfrac12mv^2=mgr$ and a minimum entry speed of $\sqrt{2gr}$. At the top, gravity alone supplies the centripetal force at the contact threshold, so the minimum speed there is $\sqrt{gr}$. For an entry speed just sufficient to maintain contact at the top, $\tfrac12mv^2-\tfrac12mgr=mg(2r)$, giving $v=\sqrt{5gr}$. The body leaves the track between mid-height and the top, so $\sqrt{2gr}<v<\sqrt{5gr}$.

perOption.A: Gives too little entry energy to reach mid-height.
perOption.B: Only reaches mid-height with zero speed.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Exceeds the minimum entry speed needed to maintain contact throughout the loop.

P and Q are on the same turntable, so they have the same angular velocity $\omega$.

explanation.body:
At P (just in contact, $N\approx0$): $mg = mv^2/r$, so $v^2 = rg$.

P and Q are at the same height, so the kinetic energy (and speed) at Q equals that at P.

explanation.body:
At the top of the circle both the weight and the tension act downwards, towards the centre, so the net (centripetal) force is $mg + T$.

questions.misconception: Using the component of weight perpendicular to the radius.

questions.stemText: The figure below shows a siren disk that has 16 holes near the edge which are equally spaced apart. When the disk is spun in front of a fast-moving jet of air, the holes modulate the air-jet to produce a sound of a particular frequency. The time it takes for successive holes to move past the air jet is the period of the sound wave. What is the angular speed of rotation if the frequency of the sound produced is 2200 Hz? A 430 rad $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ B 860 rad $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ C 1730 rad $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ D 3650 rad $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$

appearances.originalFile: grail:14610 YIJC 2024 JC2 PRELIM H2 Phy P1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: Novel context: must realise one sound period corresponds to 1/16 of a revolution.
questions.misconception: Treating the sound frequency as the rotation frequency

explanation.body:
The period of the sound wave is $T = \frac{1}{f}$, the time for the disc to turn from one hole to the next.

Angle between successive holes: $\theta = \frac{2\pi}{16} = \frac{\pi}{8}\ \mathrm{rad}$.

$\omega = \frac{\theta}{T} = \theta f = \frac{\pi}{8}(2200) = 864\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$

perOption.A: Uses $\pi/16$ instead of $2\pi/16$ for the angle between holes.
perOption.B: Correct. $\omega = (\pi/8)(2200) \approx 860\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.
perOption.C: Doubles the correct angle between holes (uses $2\pi/8$).
perOption.D: Does not divide the full-revolution angle correctly among the 16 holes.
